//Connection: How new members are admitted (ARCHITECTURE.md 5.2). Mode is one of:
Open           - anyone may register. The default.
PasswordGated  - a shared password is required to join. Existing members are unaffected
by a later change, since the password gates registration only.
AllowlistOnly  - only the public keys listed below may register.
JoinSecretHash is a HASH of the joining password, never the password itself. A
PasswordGated server with this unset admits nobody, which is the safe direction to fail.
Allowlist entries are base64url public keys - either a bare signing key or the full
shareable identity token a member sends you. Unreadable entries are ignored, not fatal.
In a container, override as Connection__Mode and Connection__JoinSecretHash.
//Setup: First-run setup (ARCHITECTURE.md 5.6). Read only while the server is unconfigured;
once setup completes these do nothing.
OwnerPublicKey pins who may claim ownership. Set it to YOUR base64url public key before
first boot and only that key can complete setup, so publishing a fresh server is safe.
Leave it null and the first client to reach setup becomes the Owner - fine on a machine
nothing else can reach, a race you can lose on a public address. The server logs a warning
on every boot while it is unset and setup is still pending.
ServerName is the name shown to members. Setup falls back to a placeholder if it is
neither set here nor supplied by the client completing setup.
//Auth: Challenge-response login (ARCHITECTURE.md 4.7). Clients prove they hold a private key by
signing a short-lived, single-use challenge; the key itself never leaves their device.
ChallengeLifetime is how long a client has to sign a challenge after asking for one. The
default covers a slow link and a device waking up. Signing itself takes microseconds, so
raising this only matters on a genuinely bad connection - it does not make login more
reliable, and a longer window is longer for a captured challenge to stay interesting.
ChallengeRetention is how long spent and expired challenges are kept before being swept.
It is not an audit trail; the rows exist so a late replay still meets a row and is refused
rather than looking like a challenge that never existed.
SessionLifetime is how long a session token is accepted after login. There is NO refresh
token: a client whose token expires simply signs another challenge, which costs one round
trip and no stored credential. Tokens are stateless, so the server cannot revoke one - this
value is the only thing that bounds how long a stolen token keeps working. Raising it widens
exactly that window; lowering it is nearly free, since clients re-authenticate silently.
ClockSkew is the tolerance allowed when checking expiry. The issuer and the validator are
the same process here, so this is deliberately far below the library default of 5 minutes.
There is no signing key to configure. The server generates its own on first use and keeps it
in the database, so there is nothing here to leak, reuse between deployments, or leave at an
example value. It is covered by a database backup like everything else - restoring an older
backup invalidates sessions issued since, and clients recover by logging in again.
All durations are formatted d.hh:mm:ss. In a container, override as Auth__ChallengeLifetime,
Auth__ChallengeRetention, Auth__SessionLifetime and Auth__ClockSkew.
